subject: physics

moments.title: Galvani's frog legs
moments.body:
Galvani is dissecting frogs and notices that their legs twitch when touched simultaneously by two different metals. He concludes the legs contain 'animal electricity' — a vital fluid intrinsic to the tissue.

His colleague Alessandro Volta disagrees. He argues the electricity comes from the dissimilar metals in contact with the moist tissue, not from anything biological.
moments.takeaway: A scientific disagreement frames the next decade of work. Volta sets out to prove the electricity is non-biological in origin.

moments.title: Volta builds the voltaic pile
moments.body:
Volta announces in a letter to the Royal Society of London a 'pile' of alternating zinc and silver discs, separated by cardboard soaked in brine. The pile produces a steady electric current — the first continuous electrical source in history.

Letter dated 20 March 1800. The Royal Society's president, Joseph Banks, reads it out and arranges publication. Within months, scientists across Europe are building larger piles and discovering new chemistry.

quote.text: I have at last constructed an apparatus which... gives the same shocks as the Leyden jar, charged to but a feeble degree, but which without any previous charge gives a shock continuously and incessantly.
quote.attrib: Alessandro Volta, letter to Sir Joseph Banks, 1800

moments.takeaway: Electricity is no longer transient sparks from rubbing or storage in Leyden jars — it flows continuously from a chemical source.

moments.title: Nicholson, Carlisle and Davy split water and isolate new metals
moments.body:
Nicholson and Carlisle (London, May 1800) use a voltaic pile to electrolyse water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen. The chemistry of water is no longer mysterious.

Humphry Davy (London, 1807-1808) uses much larger voltaic piles to isolate sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, barium and strontium for the first time. The pile opens up half of inorganic chemistry within a decade.
moments.takeaway: A new technology — continuous current — transforms chemistry. Whole branches of inorganic chemistry suddenly become possible.

moments.title: The volt is named
moments.body:
The unit of electric potential difference is named the volt in his honour at the 1881 International Electrical Congress. Volta had died in 1827.

The same congress names the ampere (Ampère), the ohm (Ohm), the coulomb (Coulomb), and the farad (Faraday). The pantheon of early electrical pioneers is enshrined in the SI.
moments.takeaway: The fundamental units of electricity are named after the people who made the subject possible.

now.title: Batteries today
now.body:
Lithium-ion batteries (developed by Whittingham 1976, Goodenough 1980, Yoshino 1985 — 2019 Nobel Prize) now power phones, laptops, electric cars and grid storage. Energy densities approach 300 Wh/kg.

Lead-acid (cars), nickel-metal-hydride (older hybrids), zinc-air (hearing aids) and many other chemistries exist. Solid-state batteries (no liquid electrolyte) are under intense development.
now.open_questions: Can battery energy density approach the gravimetric limit of about 5 kWh/kg set by Li-air or sulfur chemistry? Can production scale to meet electric vehicle and grid demands without unsustainable rare-element mining? Can recycling reach the 95+ percent recovery needed for a circular battery economy?

reflection: Galvani thought he had found a vital force; Volta proved him wrong. Both were partly right: nerves do work by electrical signalling, and Volta's pile generates current from chemistry, not biology. How often is a scientific dispute resolved by both parties being partly right, only to be remembered as a winner-takes-all?
